unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 8! This unit is all about the tools, machines, and everyday items we use at home, at school, and at work. You will learn the names of many useful objects — from a stapler and a microwave to a telescope and a helicopter. You will also learn how to describe what these things do, how to give safe instructions for using them, and how to talk about working together as a crew. By the end of the unit, you will be ready to read and enjoy this unit's mystery story, “The Attic Clue”, about a class in Rwanda who discover old tools in a dusty attic and build something amazing together.
unit.learningPath:
Start with Vocabulary and learn a few words each day from the three word groups.
Work through the six grammar lessons, from relative clauses to imperatives and connectors.
Read the four Reading and Listening texts, then enjoy the story “The Attic Clue”.
Answer the Comprehension questions, then move on through Speaking, Writing and Activities.
Finish with the unit Quiz and the Self-Assessment to see what you have learned.

readings.title: The Right Tool for the Job
readings.setting: A home and a workplace in a familiar learner context
readings.passageScript:
Every job needs the right tool, and every tool has its own special job to do. At school, when Amal wants to join her homework pages together, she reaches for a stapler instead of tape or glue, because a stapler holds pages firmly without any mess. At home, when her mother wants to heat the soup quickly before dinner, she uses the microwave rather than lighting the stove, because it warms food in just a few minutes. When her father carries his work papers to the office, he keeps them safe and tidy inside a briefcase, not loose in his hands. Even small items like a folder or a shield can be the right tool for a small job, keeping papers neat or protecting something fragile.

Big jobs need big machines and many hands working together. In a factory, heavy machinery helps people build cars and lift boxes that would be far too heavy to carry alone. On a farm, a strong crew works together with rakes, shovels, and other hardware, sharing the resources they have so that everyone finishes faster. Whether the job is tiny, like fixing a torn page, or huge, like lifting a car engine, the same rule applies. The right tool, used the right way, makes hard work easy, saves valuable time, and keeps everyone safe while they work.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: A Look at the Stars
readings.setting: A clear desert night under an open sky
readings.passageScript:
On a clear night in the desert, the sky fills with thousands of tiny, twinkling stars stretching from one dark horizon to the other. Long ago, people could only look up with their own eyes, so the moon and the planets stayed small, pale dots that nobody could study closely. Then, long ago, someone built the very first telescope — a tool made of curved glass lenses that helps us see things that are very far away as if they were much nearer.

With a telescope, you can see the craters on the moon, dotted across its grey surface like tiny bowls carved into rock. Turn the telescope towards a planet, and you might spot the rings around a planet, glowing like a thin, glittering bracelet in the dark sky. Some telescopes are small enough to carry outside in a case; others are so large that scientists build a whole observatory, a special round building with a roof that opens, just to hold them steady.

A telescope is a machine that brings the sky closer, even though the stars and planets never actually move an inch. It simply gathers more light than our eyes alone ever could, so distant, blurry shapes turn into clear, sharp pictures. Every time astronomers look through one, they learn something new, and it shows us that the world — and the whole sky above it — is bigger and more wonderful than we thought.
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: How to Use the Microwave Safely
readings.setting: A kitchen at home, with an adult nearby
readings.passageScript:
“Hello! Today I will show you how to use a microwave safely, so listen carefully before you try this at home with an adult nearby. First, put your food in a bowl or a plate that is safe for the microwave, like glass or certain plastic — check the bottom if you are not sure. Never use metal, not even a spoon or foil, because metal can cause sparks. Next, close the door firmly and set the time for your food; a small bowl of soup usually needs less time than a big plate of rice.

While the microwave is running, you have to stay close so that the food does not get too hot or bubble over the sides. This is also a good moment to find a clean utensil ready for later, so you are not searching for one with hot hands. When it beeps, do not rush — open the door carefully, because the bowl will be hot even if the food inside still looks cool! Use a cloth to take it out, never your bare fingers.

Once the bowl is safely on the table, stir the food with a clean utensil before you eat, because the middle can be much hotter than the edges. Let it cool for a moment if it is steaming. Now you know the safe steps — enjoy your warm meal!”
readings.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

readings.title: The Attic Clue
readings.setting: A village school in the green hills of Rwanda
readings.passageScript:
High in the green hills of Rwanda, a small village school sat beside tall trees and rolling farms. It had three classrooms, a dusty library, and a small attic just under the roof.
One morning, Teacher Yasmin came in carrying a big box. “This week,” she said, “we will work together as a crew. We will clean and explore the attic. Then you will write a story about what you find.”
The students gasped. The attic had been locked for years. What secrets could be up there?
“I will open it tomorrow,” said Teacher Yasmin. “But we have to wear safety equipment — gloves and masks — because the attic may be dusty.”
The next day, the students put on gloves and cloth masks. They took torches, brooms, and a folder to hold any papers they found.
Amal climbed the ladder first. “It is dark,” she said, “but it is not scary.”
Her friend Leo followed close behind. “Look — there is a big curtain covering something!”
They pulled the curtain away and found an old wooden table covered with tools: a stapler, some broken pens, and even a small telescope.
“Look at this!” said Amal. She pointed to a briefcase with stickers of aeroplanes and stars.
They opened it and found drawings of machines and a note that said: “For the student who will build the future.”
Downstairs, Teacher Yasmin smiled. “This school was started long ago by a woman who loved science. Perhaps she left this for someone special.”
“We want to build something!” said Leo.
“Then you must plan like a real team,” said Teacher Yasmin. “Choose your tools and your resources, and work together.”
The students picked their favourite items. “We will use the machinery from the old art room,” said Leo. “It still works.”
“I will clean all the parts,” said Amal, “and we will write an article about it.”
“You have to be careful with sharp things,” warned Teacher Yasmin. “Use the hardware safely.”
“We will,” the whole class promised.
That night, Amal wrote in her notebook: “We found a dusty attic and old tools. We have to clean everything. Tomorrow, we will build something useful.”
The next morning, the crew met early. They carried the parts in and cleaned the work area. Leo warmed some cocoa in the microwave to share with everyone.
“Do not forget to bring your own utensil,” said Amal. “We cannot stir it with our fingers!” She handed out spoons, and everyone laughed.
Little by little, they built a small toy helicopter. It had buttons and even a tiny shield made of plastic. “This shield is for safety!” said Leo.
They tested it outside. It lifted off, spun in the air, and landed gently on the grass.
A young boy clapped his hands. “It flies!”
“Let us write a poster,” said Amal. “We will describe what it does and how we built it.” Together they wrote:
“This is a flying machine that uses clean energy. It has a shield that protects its wires. It was built by a crew who worked hard together.”
At the school fair, parents and children came to see the project. One mother said, “My son wants to be an inventor now!”
A visiting teacher asked, “Where did you learn to do this?” Leo grinned. “In the attic!”
In the afternoon, an ambulance drove past the school. A student asked, “Who drives that?”
“Someone who helps sick people,” said Amal, “like a nurse or a doctor.” “We have to learn about safety too,” added Leo, “so that we do not need an ambulance.”
Later, the class packed up. “Put the tools in the folder,” said Teacher Yasmin, “and then clean up.”
Amal asked, “Should we wash the spoons in the sink?” “No,” said Teacher Yasmin, smiling. “Use the new dishwasher the school bought last week!” Everyone laughed — it was their first time using it.
At home that night, Amal brushed her teeth with her new toothbrush and toothpaste. She looked at her reflection and whispered, “I helped build a flying machine.”
Her mother came in. “Did you learn something today?” she asked.
“Yes,” said Amal. “I learned that tools help us — but teamwork builds the best things of all.”

comprehension.question: Which tool does Amal use to join her homework pages together?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amal uses a stapler to join her homework pages together.
comprehension.explanation: The second sentence of the text names the stapler as the tool for joining pages.

comprehension.question: According to the text, what two jobs does heavy machinery do inside a factory?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Heavy machinery helps people build cars and lift boxes.
comprehension.explanation: Both jobs sit in the same factory sentence, so give both building and lifting.

comprehension.question: Name two things the star text says you can see through a telescope.
comprehension.correctAnswer: You can see the craters on the moon and the rings around a planet.
comprehension.explanation: The middle of the passage lists both sights, so either pair of details is enough.

comprehension.question: The text says a telescope “brings the sky closer”. What does that phrase really mean?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It means the telescope makes faraway things look near; the sky does not actually move.
comprehension.explanation: This is figurative language, so you must explain the effect rather than repeat the words.

comprehension.question: Why does the speaker warn you never to put metal inside the microwave?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Metal must stay out because it can cause sparks.
comprehension.explanation: The warning and its reason are joined by because in the third sentence of the talk.

comprehension.question: What does the speaker tell you to do while the food is heating, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: You have to stay close so that the food does not get too hot.
comprehension.explanation: The talk uses have to for the rule and so that for the purpose, which is the pattern this unit teaches.

comprehension.question: Who does the song thank at the end, and what do those people do?
comprehension.correctAnswer: It thanks the people who work night and day to keep us safe.
comprehension.explanation: The last line names the workers, not the machines, so the answer must be about people.

comprehension.question: What safety equipment did Teacher Yasmin tell the crew to wear, and why?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They had to wear gloves and masks because the attic might be dusty.
comprehension.explanation: Teacher Yasmin gives the rule and the reason in the same sentence, joined by because.

comprehension.question: What did Amal and Leo find inside the briefcase in the attic?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They found drawings of machines and a note about building the future.
comprehension.explanation: The briefcase is opened one line after Amal points at it, and two things come out of it.

comprehension.question: What did the crew build from the old parts, and what was its plastic shield for?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They built a toy helicopter, and the plastic shield protected its wires.
comprehension.explanation: The poster the crew wrote explains the shield's job, so the evidence sits later than the building.

comprehension.question: What does Amal say she has learned by the last line of the story?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She learned that tools help us, but teamwork builds the best things of all.
comprehension.explanation: The closing line is Amal's own words, so the answer should quote or closely follow them.

comprehension.question: The note said, “For the student who will build the future.” What do you think the writer hoped would happen?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She hoped a future student would use her drawings and invent something new.
comprehension.explanation: This is an inference: the story never states her wish, so you must reason from the drawings she left.

grammar.title: Defining Relative Clauses (who, that, which)
grammar.explanation: A defining relative clause is an extra part of a sentence that tells us exactly which person or thing we mean. For example, in “the tool that joins papers,” the words “that joins papers” tell us it is a stapler. This helps us describe the tools and machines in this unit clearly.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
who → for people: “She is the teacher who helps us.”
which → for things and animals: “The car which is parked outside is blue.”
that → for people, animals, or things: “A machine that heats food is a microwave.”
Tip on the pattern: start with a noun, add who / that / which, then add the extra information — “The crew that worked hard finished early.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “The teacher which helps us is nice.” ✗ Fix: use who for people — “The teacher who helps us is nice.” ✓
Mistake: dropping the relative word — “The girl runs fast is my friend.” ✗ Fix: “The girl who runs fast is my friend.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Think: who for people (like a superhero), which for things (like your favourite toy), and that for almost anything.
grammar.practice: Fill in the blank with who, that, or which: | The film ______ was on TV last night was funny. | The girl ______ won the race is my sister. | I have a machine ______ heats food quickly. | The book ______ you lent me was amazing. | The nurse ______ helps sick people is kind. | Answers: 1. that / which 2. who 3. that / which 4. that / which 5. who

grammar.title: Using “have to” for Obligation
grammar.explanation: When we say we have to do something, we mean it is necessary — we must do it. This unit uses “have to” for safety rules, like wearing gloves in the attic or being careful with sharp tools.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Subject + have to / has to + the base form of the verb.
I / you / we / they → have to: “We have to wear equipment to stay safe.”
he / she / it → has to: “She has to finish her homework.”
Questions: “Do you have to go?” Negative: “I do not have to go.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “She have to clean the attic.” ✗ Fix: “She has to clean the attic.” ✓
Keep the second verb in its base form: say “have to go”, never “have to going”.
grammar.memoryTip: Picture “have to” as your must-do list on the fridge. If a job is on the list, you have to do it.

Does he have to help

grammar.title: Future Tense with “will” for Promises
grammar.explanation: We use will to talk about the future, and especially to make a promise. Saying “I will” shows that you mean to keep your word, like promising to keep your folder tidy all term.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Subject + will + the base form of the verb.
“I will keep my folder tidy.”
“We will build something useful.”
Negative: add not → “I will not forget.” Short form: “I won't forget.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “I will keeps my room tidy.” ✗ Fix: the verb after will stays in its base form — “I will keep my room tidy.” ✓
Never drop the subject: say “I will clean my room”, not “Will clean my room”.
grammar.memoryTip: Treat will as your promise helper: it stands beside the verb every time you give your word.
grammar.practice: Complete each sentence with the correct form using will: | I ______ (help) you with your project. | She ______ (not forget) to bring snacks. | They ______ (clean) the classroom tomorrow. | We ______ (be) friends forever. | Answers: 1. will help 2. will not forget (won't forget) 3. will clean 4. will be

grammar.title: The Past Simple Tense
grammar.explanation: The past simple tells about actions that already happened and are finished. It is the tense that carries a story, like the day the class found old tools in the dusty attic.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Regular verbs: add -ed → play → played, jump → jumped.
Verbs ending in -e: add just -d → like → liked.
Irregular verbs must be learned by heart → go → went, find → found, have → had.
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “I find my keys yesterday.” ✗ Fix: “I found my keys yesterday.” ✓
Irregular verbs never take -ed: “She goed to the shop.” ✗ Fix: “She went to the shop.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Hear the -ed ending as a time stamp clicking shut: whatever it lands on has already happened.
grammar.practice: Write the past simple form of the verb in brackets: | I ______ (find) a coin on the ground. | They ______ (play) games all afternoon. | She ______ (go) to the market last week. | We ______ (visit) our friends on Saturday. | He ______ (cook) breakfast this morning. | Answers: 1. found 2. played 3. went 4. visited 5. cooked

grammar.title: Personal Pronouns and Tense
grammar.explanation: Personal pronouns — I, you, he, she, it, we, they — stand in place of a noun so we do not repeat it. The verb then changes to show whether we mean the past or the future, which keeps a report clear.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Choose the pronoun that matches the person or thing: she for a girl, he for a boy, it for an object.
Past: use the past verb → “She baked biscuits.”
Future: use will + base verb → “We will travel next summer.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: “She is my brother.” ✗ Fix: a brother is a boy — “He is my brother.” ✓
Mistake: mixing two times in one sentence — “I will played football yesterday.” ✗ Fix: “I played football yesterday.” ✓
grammar.memoryTip: Pronouns are the stars of the sentence and tense is the time machine: point it back for the past, forward for the future.
grammar.practice: Fill in the correct pronoun and the right past or future verb: | ______ (I) ______ (go) to the zoo last weekend. | ______ (We) ______ (play) football tomorrow. | ______ (He) ______ (watch) a film last night. | ______ (She) ______ (finish) her homework later today. | Answers: 1. I went 2. We will play 3. He watched 4. She will finish

grammar.title: Cause and Effect Connectors (because, so that) and Imperatives
grammar.explanation: Connectors and imperatives work as a pair when we explain how to use tools. because and so that answer why and for what purpose, while an imperative gives the instruction itself, as in “Use the hardware safely so that nobody is hurt.”
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
because → gives the reason: “She was late because she missed the bus.”
so that → gives the purpose: “I study hard so that I can pass my exams.”
Imperatives start with the base verb and need no subject: “Clean your room.”
Add detail: “Carry the books to the library.” Be polite with please: “Please put your shoes away.” Say do not for a negative: “Do not run in the corridor.”
grammar.commonMistake:
Mistake: leaving the connector out — “He wore a mask it was dusty.” ✗ Fix: “He wore a mask because it was dusty.” ✓
Mistake: adding an ‘s’ to a command — “Uses your utensils properly.” ✗ Fix: “Use your utensils properly.” ✓ An imperative also needs no subject, so say “Clean your room” rather than “You clean your room”.
grammar.memoryTip: because answers “Why?” and so that answers “For what purpose?”; an imperative is simply a verb handing someone a job.
grammar.practice: Part A — fill in the blank with because or so that: | I bring my umbrella ______ it might rain. | She went to bed early ______ she could wake up fresh. | He loves to paint ______ it makes him happy. | They wore helmets ______ they would be safe while cycling. | Part B — write the correct imperative using the verb in brackets: | ______ your hands before eating. (Wash) | ______ your toys after playing. (Put away) | ______ your homework every day. (Complete) | ______ carefully with the sharp hardware. (Work) | Answers, Part A: 1. because 2. so that 3. because 4. so that | Answers, Part B: 1. Wash 2. Put away 3. Complete 4. Work

writing.title: Writing 1: An Object Description Poster
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Choose a useful tool or item (for example a stapler, a shield, or a microwave). Draw it, then write three sentences about it. Use at least one adjective and one relative clause:
“This is my microwave. It is a white machine that heats food quickly. I use it to warm my soup.”
writing.modelText: This is my red stapler. It is a small metal tool that presses a thin clip through my pages. I use it to join my homework sheets so that they stay tidy in my folder. My mum says it is the most useful piece of equipment on my desk.

items: Object: This is my red stapler.
Description: It is a small metal tool that presses a thin clip through my pages.
Use: I use it to join my homework sheets so that they stay tidy in my folder.

writing.successCriteria: I named my object; I used at least one adjective; I wrote one relative clause with that, who or which; I checked capital letters and full stops.
writing.support: Say the sentence aloud first, then write it: name it, describe it, explain what it does.
writing.extension: Add a fourth sentence explaining what you would do if the object broke.

writing.title: Writing 2: Instructions: How to Use It Safely
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write four steps to explain how to use one tool or machine safely. Use imperatives and have to:
Title: “How to Use a ______ Safely”
Step 1: ______. Step 2: ______. Step 3: ______. Step 4: ______.
Include one sentence with “You have to ______ so that ______.”
writing.modelText:
How to Use a Microwave Safely
1. Put your food in a glass or plastic bowl, never a metal one.
2. Close the door firmly and set the time.
3. Stay close while it is running. You have to watch the bowl so that the soup does not bubble over.
4. Take the bowl out carefully with a cloth and stir it with a clean utensil.

items: Title: How to Use a Microwave Safely
Step 1: Put your food in a glass or plastic bowl, never a metal one.
Step 2: Close the door firmly and set the time.
Step 3: Stay close while it is running. You have to watch the bowl so that the soup does not bubble over.
Step 4: Take the bowl out carefully with a cloth and stir it with a clean utensil.

writing.successCriteria: I gave a clear title; every step began with a command word; my steps are in the right order; I used have to and so that once.
writing.support: Do the task in real life first, saying each step aloud before you write it down.
writing.extension: Add a warning line that begins with Never or Do not, and explain the danger.

writing.title: Writing 4: Connected Paragraph
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a six-sentence paragraph about the crew in “The Attic Clue”. Begin with a topic sentence, join ideas with and, but and because, and finish by saying what the crew learned.
writing.modelText: The crew in the story worked well because everyone had a job. Teacher Yasmin gave out gloves and masks, and the students carried torches and brooms up to the attic. It was dark and dusty, but nobody was scared. Amal swept the floor, and Leo held the torch so that she could see. They found an old box, but they waited for their teacher because the attic clue was for everyone. The crew learned that hard work is safer and quicker when you do it together.

items: Sentence 1 (topic sentence): The crew in the story worked well because everyone had a job.
Sentence 2: Teacher Yasmin gave out gloves and masks, and the students carried torches and brooms up to the attic.
Sentence 3: It was dark and dusty, but nobody was scared.
Sentence 4: Amal swept the floor, and Leo held the torch so that she could see.
Sentence 5: They found an old box, but they waited for their teacher because the attic clue was for everyone.
Sentence 6 (closing): The crew learned that hard work is safer and quicker when you do it together.

writing.successCriteria: My first sentence gave the main idea; I used and, but and because at least once each; my last sentence said what the crew learned.
writing.support: List the six ideas as short notes before you turn them into sentences.
writing.extension: Replace two ordinary verbs with stronger ones, such as hurried instead of went.

writing.title: Writing 5: Information Text
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an information text called “Three Machines That Help Us”. Give it a heading, then write five accurate facts about the microwave, the helicopter and the ambulance, using precise unit words.
writing.modelText:
Three Machines That Help Us
A microwave is a machine that heats food in a few minutes. You have to use a glass or plastic bowl in it, because metal can cause sparks. A helicopter has spinning blades on top, so it can fly straight up and land in small places. An ambulance is a vehicle that carries sick people to hospital quickly. Its loud siren tells other drivers to move aside so that it can arrive in time.
writing.sentenceStarter: Three machines that help us are...

items: Heading: Three Machines That Help Us
Fact 1: A microwave is a machine that heats food in a few minutes.
Fact 2: You have to use a glass or plastic bowl in a microwave, because metal can cause sparks.
Fact 3: A helicopter has spinning blades on top, so it can fly straight up and land in small places.
Fact 4: An ambulance is a vehicle that carries sick people to hospital quickly.
Fact 5: An ambulance's loud siren tells other drivers to move aside so that it can arrive in time.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote a clear heading; all five facts are true; I used at least three unit words correctly; I checked my spelling.
writing.support: Reread the star text and the microwave talk, and note one fact from each before you write.
writing.extension: Add a numbered list of two safety rules under your facts.

writing.title: Writing 6: Reflect and Improve
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Reread your object poster and your safety instructions. Revise three sentences, add two useful details from the Word Wall, and explain in one sentence which change helped your reader most.
writing.modelText: I changed "This is my thing that keeps papers" to "This is my blue folder that keeps my papers flat." I changed "Put the food in" to "Put the food in a plastic bowl." I changed "Be careful" to "Stay close so that the soup does not boil over." I added the Word Wall words folder and plastic. The change that helped my reader most was naming the folder, because now they can picture the exact object instead of just any thing.
writing.sentenceStarter: The change that helped my reader most was...

items: Revision 1: I changed "This is my thing that keeps papers" to "This is my blue folder that keeps my papers flat."
Revision 2: I changed "Put the food in" to "Put the food in a plastic bowl."
Revision 3: I changed "Be careful" to "Stay close so that the soup does not boil over."
Word Wall words added: folder and plastic.
The change that helped my reader most was naming the folder, because now they can picture the exact object instead of just any thing.
otherAnswers: The change that helped my reader most was adding the plastic bowl detail, because now the reader knows exactly what to use instead of guessing.
The change that helped my reader most was changing "Be careful" to "Stay close so that the soup does not boil over", because now the reader knows exactly what to do to stay safe.

writing.successCriteria: I revised three sentences; I added two Word Wall words; I explained one improvement and why it helped.
writing.support: Read your first draft aloud and mark every place where a listener looked puzzled.

teacherNotes.note: Model each new machine word aloud with its picture before independent work, and check meaning by asking learners to mime the object's job. An adult must stay present whenever a learner uses the AI tutor or a recording device, and no child should be left alone with the device. Give feedback on complete sentences, evidence from the text and precise vocabulary rather than on effort alone.

Use these source-linked tutor questions to steer AI English sessions, always with an adult sitting alongside the learner.
Reading and listening: ask the tutor to read the microwave talk with the learner and help list the steps, then to explain any unfamiliar word from the two reading texts.
Speaking: ask the tutor to play What Am I?, to check that the learner's have to sentences are accurate, and to help build a description with that or which.
Writing: ask the tutor to review the object poster, to judge whether the safety instructions are in a sensible order, and to help make the will promises polite and clear.
Vocabulary: ask the tutor to quiz the tool group, to explain the difference between hardware and machinery, and to quiz the household and transport groups.
Grammar: ask the tutor to check the practice answers and to explain why we say she has to but we have to.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 1. c 2. a 3. d 4. b. If a learner pairs the telescope with hospital work, ask which machine looks upward at the night sky.
1. ingredient 2. shield 3. attic 4. machinery. Point out that machinery is uncountable here, which is why the sentence says helps and not help.
1. that (or which) 2. who 3. that (or which). Accept which for the machine and the briefcase, but not who, because both are things.
There is no single correct choice. Award the mark when the learner names one item, gives a reason with because, and adds a purpose with so that.
Any three defensible groups are correct, for example office tools, kitchen items and vehicles. Check that the rule sentence is true of every word the learner placed in that group.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Six details copied accurately and labelled with their text. A strong explanation says, for example, that the sparks warning tells the reader exactly why metal is dangerous.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: The microwave. If a learner picks the toothpaste, ask which of the four options plugs into the wall.
machinery. Machinery is the collective word for big working machines; crew is the collective word for people.
folder. Remind the learner that the crew needed something to hold loose papers, not something that flies or magnifies.
Its craters. Craters are the round dents on the moon's surface, named directly in the star text.
She has to clean the attic. Two errors are being tested at once: the wrong form of have, and the -ing ending on the second verb.
who. If a learner chooses which, remind them that a crew is made of people, and people take who.
Wash your hands before you eat. Ask the learner to find the subject in each option; the imperative is the only one without one.
shield. The shield in the story is the plastic guard over the toy helicopter's wires.
utensil. The talk suggests stirring with a spoon, and a spoon is one kind of utensil.
She went to the market last week. Goed is a common and reasonable over-generalisation; praise the pattern spotting, then teach went.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Tools, Machines, and Everyday Items" — new words, a grammar focus, and a story. See exactly what they will practise below.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 8-9 years old and is building on English they already know. So YOU lead this unit alongside them — a teacher in class or a parent at home.

Work in short, regular sessions rather than one long one. Reading together, saying words out loud, and playing with the grammar patterns matter more than getting every answer right first time.

This guide tells you what the unit covers and how to go through it together. The learner's own pages (Reading & story, Grammar, Activities) are what your child works through on screen.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
The AI Tutor is there for extra practice and conversation — a grown-up should still be nearby, especially the first few times.

Ask the tutor to say a word slowly so your child can copy it: "Please say the word 'equipment' slowly."

Ask it to make up a short question using this unit's words, or to listen to your child's sentence and say if it sounds right.

Ask it for one more practice question if your child wants to keep going after the unit is finished.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for teaching this unit
sections.body:
Keep sessions short and positive. Stop while it is still enjoyable, not after it has become a chore.

Say new words and example sentences out loud yourselves — hearing English spoken, not just reading it, is what builds confidence.

Let your child make mistakes without worrying. Gently model the correct version rather than correcting every slip.

Praise effort and progress, not just correct answers — confidence carries a learner further than perfect grammar at this stage.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Name and describe many tools, machines, and everyday items in English.
Describe an object using adjectives and a relative clause with who, that, or which.
Say what people have to do to stay safe when using tools and machines.
Make promises about the future using will.
Tell a short story about the past using the past simple tense.
Give clear instructions using imperatives, like “Use”, “Put”, and “Clean”.
Explain reasons using because and so that.

sections.title: Words We Will Learn
items: Tools and Equipment: equipment · folder · briefcase · shield · stapler · hardware · machinery · resources
Household and Personal Items: curtain · ingredient · cocoa · microwave · utensil · toothbrush · toothpaste · attic · plastic
Work and Transport: crew · telescope · helicopter · ambulance

sections.title: How to Teach This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
Repeat this simple shape over one or two short sessions:

1. Warm-up (2-3 min)
Say hello in English together and ask what your child remembers from the last unit.

2. Learn the words (5-10 min)
Go through Tools and Equipment, Household and Personal Items, Work and Transport, a few words at a time. Say each word, then have your child repeat it and use it in a short sentence.

3. Grammar and practice (5-10 min)
Look at "Defining Relative Clauses (who, that, which)" together and try a few lines of its practice out loud.

4. Story and listening time (5 min)
Read or listen to "The Attic Clue" together, and enjoy "How to Use the Microwave Safely" too.

5. Activity time (5-10 min)
Sit with your child and do "Activities 1: Match the Tool to the Job" together, reading each instruction aloud for them if needed.

6. Wrap-up (2 min)
Ask what they learned today and celebrate with a “Well done!”

sections.title: Sentence Patterns to Say Out Loud
items: She is the teacher who helps us.
We have to wear equipment to stay safe.
I will keep my folder tidy.
She baked biscuits.
She was late because she missed the bus.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. Just watch for these as you go through the unit together:
items: All twenty-one Word Wall words ticked, plus six items named correctly in the Activities 1 matching task.
A Writing 1 poster and a Speaking 1 riddle that each contain one accurate relative clause with who, that or which.
Three recorded safety rules in Speaking 2 that use have to or has to accurately for the subject.
Two written promises in Writing 3 that use will with a base verb and name a real object from the unit.
A retelling of “The Attic Clue” in Writing 4 with at least five past simple verbs, including two irregular ones.
A four-step safety guide in Writing 2 where every step opens with a base-form command verb.
Answers to Activities 4 and comprehension question twelve that give a because reason and a so that purpose.
